Time series part1

Time series

introduction

set.seed(123)

# Trend
trend <- 1:100 + rnorm(100, 0, 5)
pi=22/7
# Seasonality
time <- 1:100
seasonal <- 10 * sin(2 * pi * time / 12) + rnorm(100, 0, 2)

# Noise
noise <- rnorm(100)

# Trend + Seasonality
trend_season <- 1:100 + 10 * sin(2 * pi * time / 12) + rnorm(100, 0, 5)

# Random Walk
random_walk <- cumsum(rnorm(100))

# Plot function
library(ggplot2)
plot_ts <- function(y, title = "") {
  ggplot(data.frame(x = 1:length(y), y = y), aes(x, y)) +
    geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.title = element_blank(),
          axis.text = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks = element_blank(),
          plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) +
    ggtitle(title)
}

plot_ts(trend)

plot_ts(seasonal)

plot_ts(noise)

plot_ts(trend_season)

plot_ts(random_walk)

Trend: The overall motion of the series. It may be consistently increasing overtime, decreasing overtime or a combination of both.

seasonality: Any regular seasonal pattern in the series. We expect ice cream sales to be higher in the summer months and lower in winter months

Residual/ Remainder: This is the bit that is left over after we take into account the trend and seasonality. It can also be thought of as a statistical noise.

Auto regressive (AR) model

  • uses past values to predict future
  • order of AR model denoted by p AR(1), AR(2), etc
  • p=no: of lagged observations AR(p) is defined as

\[y_t=c + \phi y_{t-1} + \phi y_{t-2}+ \phi y_{t-3}+ ..... + \epsilon_t\]

\(\epsilon_t\) is white noise.
c is the constant term.
\(\phi\) is the parameter of the model.
\(y_{t-1}\), \(y_{t-2}\) are the past values.

\[AR(2)=c+ \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2}\] \[ AR(1)=c+\phi_1 y_{t-1}\]

Moving Average (MA) model

  • uses the past error terms (residual)
  • order of the MA(q)
  • q= no of lagged error terms. which is different from moving average smoothing technique

\[ y_t=\epsilon+\theta_1 \epsilon_{t-1}+\theta_2 \epsilon_{t-2}.....\]

https://www.icicidirect.com/futures-and-options/articles/what-is-moving-averages-and-how-does-it-help-in-technical-analysis

\(\theta_1=?\)
\(\theta_2=?\)

AutoRegressive Moving Average (ARMA)

  • COMBINES AR & MA model for forecasting

  • captures both temporal dependencies and error terms

  • order (p,q)

  • ARMA(p,q)

\[=c+ \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} c+\phi_1 y_{t-1}+...........+\theta_1 \epsilon_{t-1}+\theta_2 \epsilon_{t-2}+.....\]

ARIMA

  • In this model I is added which is “INTEGRATED”.

  • difference order

  • ARIMA(p,d,q)

  • p (from AR model)

  • d (difference),

  • q (from MA model))

    \[ \Delta y_t= \phi_1 \Delta y_{t-1}+ \phi_2 \Delta y_{t-2}+..... + \]

    remaning terms as like ARMA

SARIMA

  • S stands for Seasonality
  • so it is Seasonal ARIMA model
  • SARIMA (p,d,q) (P,D,Q) M
  • (p,d,q) order of ARIMA
  • (P,D,Q) order of seasonal part
  • m period

stationarity vs. non-stationarity

constant variance through time, constant mean through time.

“Imagine you’re standing on a flat treadmill — you keep walking, but your view doesn’t change much over time. That’s a stationary process — things vary, but their average and spread stay constant.

Now imagine walking uphill — even if your pace is steady, your elevation keeps increasing. That’s non-stationary — the data has a trend.”

You can also compare to:

Weather vs. climate: daily temperature fluctuates (stationary around a mean), but long-term warming (non-stationary).

Student grades: if the class average stays the same every semester → stationary; if it keeps improving over years → non-stationary.

Concept What it Means How to Spot It
Stationary Mean, variance, and autocovariance do not change over time Data fluctuates around a constant level
Non-stationary Mean or variance changes over time Upward/downward trend, changing spread, or seasonality

Use AirPassengers data (non-stationary)

data("AirPassengers")
plot(AirPassengers, main="Monthly Air Passengers (1949–1960)", col="steelblue")

  • Do you see a trend? (Upward)

  • Is the variability constant? (No — it grows with time)

Check stationarity formally with ADF test

Augmented Dickey–Fuller test (ADF)

library(tseries)
adf.test(AirPassengers,k=7)
## Warning in adf.test(AirPassengers, k = 7): p-value smaller than printed p-value
## 
##  Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test
## 
## data:  AirPassengers
## Dickey-Fuller = -7.3689, Lag order = 7, p-value = 0.01
## alternative hypothesis: stationary
adf.test(diff(AirPassengers))
## Warning in adf.test(diff(AirPassengers)): p-value smaller than printed p-value
## 
##  Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test
## 
## data:  diff(AirPassengers)
## Dickey-Fuller = -7.0177, Lag order = 5, p-value = 0.01
## alternative hypothesis: stationary

The p-value will be high → non-stationary.

Make it stationary

Log-transform to stabilize variance:

log_ap <- log(AirPassengers)
plot(log_ap, main="Log-Transformed AirPassengers")

Difference to remove trend:

diff_log_ap <- diff(log_ap)
plot(diff_log_ap, main="1st Differenced Log(AirPassengers)")

adf.test(diff_log_ap)
## Warning in adf.test(diff_log_ap): p-value smaller than printed p-value
## 
##  Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test
## 
## data:  diff_log_ap
## Dickey-Fuller = -6.4313, Lag order = 5, p-value = 0.01
## alternative hypothesis: stationary

In Augmented Dickey–Fuller (ADF) test:

Null hypothesis (H₀): the series is non-stationary (has a unit root).

Alternative hypothesis (H₁): the series is stationary.

So:

High p-value (> 0.05) → Fail to reject H₀ → likely non-stationary.

Low p-value (< 0.05) → Reject H₀ → likely stationary.

Thus, after differencing:

“The warning actually tells us the transformation worked — our data is now stationary!”

Concept Key Idea R Example
Stationary Mean, variance constant over time rnorm(100)
Non-stationary Trend, seasonality, or changing variance AirPassengers
Why it matters Many models (ARIMA, ETS) assume stationarity
How to fix it Differencing, detrending, logging 
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)
time <- 1:100

# Stationary (white noise)
stationary <- rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Non-stationary (with trend)
nonstationary <- cumsum(rnorm(100, mean = 0.3, sd = 1))

# Plot
df <- data.frame(time, stationary, nonstationary)

ggplot(df, aes(time)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = stationary), color = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = nonstationary + 10), color = "firebrick") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Stationary (blue) vs Non-Stationary (red, shifted for visibility)",
       x = "Time", y = "Value")

#install.packages("forecast")
library(forecast)
data("AirPassengers")
class(AirPassengers)
## [1] "ts"
start(AirPassengers)

## [1] 1960   12
frequency(AirPassengers)
## [1] 12
tsdata<-ts(AirPassengers,frequency = 12)
ddata<-decompose(tsdata,"multiplicative")
plot(ddata)

plot(ddata$seasonal)

plot(ddata$trend)

plot(ddata$random)

plot(ddata$x)

Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

The ACF plots the correlation of the time series with itself at different lags. This helps in identifying patterns such as seasonality, trends, and the persistence of values over time.

  • Lag 1: Correlation between observations at time t and t−1

  • Lag 2: Correlation between observations at time t and t−2

  • And so on…

Partial Autocorrelation

Partial autocorrelation measures the correlation between observations at two time points, accounting for the values of the observations at all shorter lags. This helps isolate the direct relationship between observations at different lags, removing the influence of intermediary observations.

Autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation helps us detect certain features in our series to enable us to choose the most optimal forecast model for our data.

example

ACF = how well you know your friend’s mood by remembering all past moods together

PACF = how well you know their mood using only the mood from exactly k days ago, ignoring other days in between

Interpreting PACF Plots

The PACF plot helps determine the order of an autoregressive model (AR model).

  • Significant Lag: A significant spike at a particular lag suggests the inclusion of that lag in the AR model.

  • Cut-off Point: The lag at which the PACF plot cuts off helps determine the maximum lag to include in the AR model.

acf(ts(mymodel$residuals), main="ACF Residual")

pacf(ts(mymodel$residuals),main="PACF residual")

myforecast<-forecast(mymodel,level=c(95), h=10.12)
#plot(myforcast)
acf(AirPassengers, main="ACF Residual")

set.seed(123)
library(forecast)

# Simulate an AR(1) series
ar1 <- arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.7), n = 100)
plot(ar1)

par(mfrow=c(1,3))
plot(ar1)
acf(ar1, main="ACF of AR(1)")
pacf(ar1, main="PACF of AR(1)")

ar2 <- arima.sim(model = list(ar = c(0.7,-0.8)), n = 100)
#plot(ar2)
par(mfrow=c(1,3))
plot(ar1)
acf(ar2, main="ACF of AR(2)")
pacf(ar2, main="PACF of AR(2)")

ma1 <- arima.sim(model = list(ma = 0.7), n = 100)
par(mfrow=c(1,3))
plot(ma1)
acf(ma1, main="ACF of MA(1)")
pacf(ma1, main="PACF of MA(1)")

ma2 <- arima.sim(model = list(ma = c(0.7,0.5)), n = 100)
par(mfrow=c(1,3))
plot(ma2)
acf(ma2, main="ACF of MA(2)")
pacf(ma2, main="PACF of MA(2)")

Full program

# -------------------------------------------
# Forecasting Airline Passengers using ARIMA
# -------------------------------------------

# Load required package
library(forecast)

# Load built-in AirPassengers dataset
data("AirPassengers")
ts_data <- AirPassengers

# View the basic structure
print(start(ts_data))
## [1] 1949    1
print(end(ts_data))
## [1] 1960   12
print(frequency(ts_data))
## [1] 12
# Plot the original data
plot(ts_data, 
     main = "Monthly Air Passengers (1949–1960)",
     ylab = "Number of Passengers (in thousands)", 
     xlab = "Year",
     col = "blue")

# Convert to logarithmic scale to stabilize variance
log_ts <- log(ts_data)

# Use auto.arima() to find the best ARIMA model automatically
fit <- auto.arima(log_ts)

# Display the model summary
summary(fit)
## Series: log_ts 
## ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)[12] 
## 
## Coefficients:
##           ma1     sma1
##       -0.4018  -0.5569
## s.e.   0.0896   0.0731
## 
## sigma^2 = 0.001371:  log likelihood = 244.7
## AIC=-483.4   AICc=-483.21   BIC=-474.77
## 
## Training set error measures:
##                        ME       RMSE        MAE        MPE      MAPE      MASE
## Training set 0.0005730622 0.03504883 0.02626034 0.01098898 0.4752815 0.2169522
##                    ACF1
## Training set 0.01443892
# Forecast the next 24 months (2 years)
future_forecast <- forecast(fit, h = 24)

# Plot the forecast (in log scale)
autoplot(future_forecast) + 
  ggtitle("Forecast of Air Passengers (log scale)") + 
  ylab("log(Passengers)")

# Convert forecast back to original scale (exponentiate)
future_forecast$mean <- exp(future_forecast$mean)
future_forecast$lower <- exp(future_forecast$lower)
future_forecast$upper <- exp(future_forecast$upper)

# Plot forecast on original scale
autoplot(future_forecast) +
  ggtitle("Forecast of Future Air Passengers (Original Scale)") +
  ylab("Number of Passengers") +
  xlab("Year")

# Print forecasted passenger numbers
print(future_forecast)
